On a rare cold-wave weekend, the family drives up Hehuan Mountain hoping to see snow. {name} waits and waits in the cold fog, almost giving up, until the very first snowflakes drift down and land on {his} mitten like tiny stars.

{name} joins a special night tour at the zoo with a keeper named Ah-Ming. With red flashlights, they watch the pangolin dig, the leopard cat stretch, and the owls glide. {name} learns that many animals wake up when people go to sleep.

After the rain, {name} and Grandpa walk in the forest and find a circle of little mushrooms. {name} imagines a tiny mushroom village with snail mail carriers and beetle buses. They only look and never pick, leaving the village safe for its tiny neighbors.

{name} builds a paper rocket and dreams of flying to the moon. At bedtime, {name} imagines floating past sleepy stars, waving at the moon rabbit, and gently landing back in bed, where the paper rocket waits on the windowsill.

At low tide on the northeast coast, {name} explores tide pools with Mom. A small crab family hides under a rock. {name} learns to look gently, put rocks back the way they were, and leaves the crabs happily at home when the tide comes in.

{name}'s new kite keeps crashing into the grass. An elderly kite flyer shows {him} how to feel the wind and run at the right moment. After many tries, the kite rises higher and higher, and {name} feels the wind tugging like a friend.

It's raining all weekend, and {name} is bored. Dad brings out a giant cardboard box, and they turn it into a pirate ship with paper sails. {name} sails across the living room sea, rescuing stuffed animals until the sun peeks out.

{name} visits Auntie's tea farm in the mountains and wants to pick leaves like the workers. {name}'s first basket is full of the wrong leaves, but after learning 'one bud, two leaves', {name} picks carefully and gets to taste the tea {he} helped make.

On the MRT, {name} notices an old man left his umbrella on the seat. {name} and Mom chase after him through the busy station, follow the signs, and catch him at the exit. The man smiles and tells them the umbrella was a gift from his late wife.

For the science fair, {name} grows bean sprouts in different lights. Halfway through, most of them die. Instead of giving up, {name} writes down what went wrong, starts again, and presents both the failure and the new results, earning the class's loudest applause.

{name} spends a night at the lighthouse where Grandma once worked as a keeper. Grandma tells stories of ships guided home through storms. As the beam sweeps slowly across the dark sea, {name} drifts to sleep feeling guided home too.

At the zoo, a baby tapir with watermelon stripes needs a name. {name} draws a picture and suggests 'Little Watermelon'. The keepers love it, and {name} waves goodbye to the baby tapir munching leaves beside its mother.

A young ant finds a big rice ball and boasts that it's all his own luck. {name} follows the crumbs back with him, and they meet the farmer who planted the rice, the rain that watered it and the sun that ripened it. The ant decides the first bite should be a thank-you, and carries a crumb back to each helper.

On the walk home, {name} and Dad play the thank-you game: thank you, bus driver; thank you, street sweeper; thank you, fruit auntie. Every thank-you makes someone smile. The very last thank-you goes to Dad, and his smile is the biggest of all.

{name} grumbles that Grandpa's old black umbrella is ugly and patched. On a rainy walk, Grandpa tells how he carried that same umbrella to school for {name}'s mom every rainy day, fixing it again and again. {name} sees the patches differently and makes Grandpa a thank-you card shaped like the umbrella.

{name} starts a secret investigation: who waters the school garden, mends the torn library books and opens the gate before sunrise? The clues lead to quiet helpers all over the school. {name}'s class plans a surprise thank-you morning, and the helpers' faces are the best clue of all.

A little cloud over the park is raining big drops, and everyone runs away. {name} looks up and asks, 'Are you sad?' The cloud was lonely. {name} stays and sings to it, and the cloud's tears turn into a small, shy rainbow.

In the forest, the big lion roars at everyone, and the animals whisper that he is mean. {name} notices he keeps lifting one front paw. Instead of running away, {name} gently asks what hurts and finds a thorn. Once it's out, the lion's roar turns into a thank-you, and the animals learn to look closer before calling someone mean.

A new classmate who just moved from Vietnam eats lunch alone and doesn't say a word. {name} remembers how lost it felt on the first day in a new class, sits down beside her, and they find a way to talk with drawings, gestures and a shared love of mango.

Old Mr. Lin downstairs shouts at kids who bounce balls in the hallway, and everyone calls him Grumpy Lin. {name} finds out he works night shifts and sleeps during the day, and that his hands shake when he carries groceries up the stairs. {name} comes up with a plan that makes the hallway better for everyone.

A little snail wants to watch the sunrise from the top of the mountain. The hare laughs that it will take forever. The snail climbs a little every day, resting when tired. Hiking with family, {name} meets the snail on the trail and cheers it on, and at dawn they watch the sunrise from the top together.

{name} plants a sunflower seed and wants it to be as tall as the window right away. Every morning {name} waters it and measures it with a paper strip. Some days nothing seems to happen. Little by little, leaf by leaf, it grows, until one morning a bright yellow face is looking in at {name}.

{name}'s class has a jump-rope challenge, and {name} trips on the rope every time, while friends seem to jump forever. {name} wants to quit, then practices at home with Dad: first just one jump, then three, counting out loud. On challenge day {name} jumps twenty times, and is proudest of all the falls that came before.

Grandpa teaches {name} calligraphy, starting with the character 永, which holds all eight basic brush strokes. {name}'s strokes come out wobbly and blotchy, page after page. Grandpa shows {name} his own first practice sheets from long ago, just as wobbly. One stroke a day, {name} keeps going, and by New Year {name}'s 永 hangs proudly on the wall.

The river bridge is broken, and the animals agree someone should ask Old Bear, who knows how to fix bridges but is known to be grumpy. Nobody wants to go. Little Mouse is scared but goes anyway, with {name} beside her and wise Grandpa Turtle walking with them. Old Bear turns out to be gruff but kind, and by sunset the bridge is mended.

At the beach, {name} is scared to put {his} face in the water. With Mom holding {him} tight, {name} blows one tiny bubble, then two, then three. At last {name} floats like a starfish in Mom's arms, and the waves feel like a giggle.

When classmates laugh at a boy who stutters, {name} feels a heart-thumping fear. {name} says, 'That's not funny,' stands beside him, and later tells the teacher. {name}'s knees were shaking the whole time, and it was the bravest thing {name} has ever done.

On a class night hike, the teacher stops at a fork to check the map while the class waits. {name} notices the trail marker points the other way, but everyone else seems sure. Speaking up could mean looking silly. {name} raises a hand anyway and points out the marker, and the teacher thanks {name} for being brave enough to say so.

{name} gets to take the class goldfish, Bubbles, home for the holiday week. It's harder than it looks: feeding at the same time every day, checking the water, remembering even on the fun day at the park. When school starts again, Bubbles is shiny and happy, and so is {name}.

{name}'s ball knocks over a neighbor's flowerpot, and no one saw. {name} could just walk away. Instead {name} knocks on the door, says what happened, and spends Saturday helping repot the flower with saved pocket money. The neighbor gives {name} a cutting to grow at home.

All summer the ants carry seeds while Grasshopper plays music and laughs at them. {name} helps the ants and also enjoys Grasshopper's songs. When winter comes, a cold, hungry Grasshopper knocks on the ants' door. The ants share their food, and next summer Grasshopper plays music while carrying seeds too.

Chosen as captain of the class vegetable garden, {name} enjoys giving orders, until the tomatoes wilt over a weekend nobody planned for. {name} realizes a captain's real job is making sure every part is covered, makes a new watering rota with the class, and signs up for the first weekend.

In winter, Rabbit shared her carrots with Little Bear, and Bear promised her the first honey of spring. When spring comes, the honey is so sweet that Bear wants it all. {name} reminds Bear of the cold days and Rabbit's carrots. Bear saves the biggest piece, and Rabbit's happy face tastes even sweeter than honey.

{name} pinky-promises little sister a tea party after nap time. Then a friend calls to invite {name} to play. {name} remembers the promise, keeps it, and invites the friend to the tea party too. Three cups, one teddy bear, and a very happy little sister.

{name} borrows a friend's favorite comic book and promises to return it on Friday, just like new. On Thursday, juice spills on the cover. {name} could hide it or make an excuse, but tells the friend the truth on Friday, and they spend lunch drying and pressing the pages together.

{name} promises a younger cousin to finish the ladder for the backyard treehouse before summer ends. Grandpa does the sawing and hammering while {name} measures, sands and paints, but it takes longer than planned. Instead of giving up or pretending, {name} tells the cousin honestly how it's going and asks Grandpa for extra afternoons. On the last day of summer, they climb up together.

A baby zebra is born with spots instead of stripes, and the other zebras don't know what to think. {name} visits the zoo and says the spots look like stars. The baby zebra plays hide-and-seek with the giraffes, and everyone discovers that spots are wonderful too.
In the crayon box, Red says red is best, and Blue says blue is best. {name} picks them all up and draws a rainbow. Every color has its own place, and the rainbow needs every one.

{name}'s new friend Wei uses a wheelchair, and the playground tag game leaves him on the side. {name} and Wei invent a new game with chalk circles and passwords that everyone can play, and soon the whole class wants to join in.

The birds tell Bat he isn't a bird, and the forest animals tell him he isn't one of them. On the night of the forest's moon picnic, a lantern goes out and everyone gets lost in the dark. Bat, who can find his way by sound, guides them home with {name}, and the animals find room for him in both groups.

On a beach clean-up with Dad, {name} spots a sea turtle resting near a pile of plastic bags. The ranger explains that turtles can mistake floating bags for jellyfish. {name} fills a whole bag with litter, and the turtle slides safely back into the clean blue sea.

The old banyan tree in the park gives shade to grandparents, swings to children and homes to birds and squirrels. When the town talks about cutting it down for a parking lot, the animals and {name} show everyone what the tree gives each day, and the town builds the parking lot around it instead.

{name} and Grandma plant little flowers on the balcony. Buzz, buzz! Bees come to visit. {name} learns to watch gently with quiet hands, and the bees dance from flower to flower like tiny yellow friends.

When the reservoir runs low in a dry summer, {name} and a friend become rain detectives. They track every drip at school, set up covered rain buckets for the plants that the janitor helps empty and clean every week, and design posters for a two-minute shower challenge. By autumn, their school has saved enough water to fill a swimming pool.

Grandpa grows a giant turnip, but he can't pull it up. Grandma pulls Grandpa, {name} pulls Grandma, the dog pulls {name}, the cat pulls the dog, and the tiny mouse pulls the cat. Heave-ho! Out pops the turnip, and everyone shares turnip soup.

A rain puddle cuts the ants off from their home. One ant alone can't move a leaf, but together they carry a long leaf across the water like a bridge. {name}, kneeling to watch, holds the leaf steady at one end, and the ants march home in a happy line.

{name}'s class is putting on a play, and everyone wants to be the star. The first rehearsal is a mess of arguing. {name} suggests that each person shares one idea, and the quiet kid's idea for the sound effects turns out to be the best part of the show.

On a snowy trip, {name} draws up a grand plan for a snow fort and bosses everyone around, but the walls keep falling. When {name} finally listens, one friend knows how to pack snow bricks, another finds the perfect windbreak, and together they build a fort big enough for the whole group.

{name} has painted a picture of the family for Mom's birthday, and a classmate knocks the water cup over it. {name} feels angry and says so. The classmate says sorry and, the next day, brings paper and paints to help make a new card. {name} decides to forgive, and the new birthday card has the whole family plus one new friend waving in the corner.

Crow takes twigs from Sparrow's half-built nest because he is in a hurry. Sparrow is upset and tells him how it felt. Crow brings the twigs back, plus some soft feathers, and says sorry. With {name}'s help, Sparrow decides to forgive, and by evening both nests are finished side by side.

{name}'s little brother wants to hold the shiny birthday balloon just for a minute, and oops, it floats away over the rooftops. {name} is furious and wants to shout. After a deep breath, {name} tells him how sad it feels, and he says a tiny sorry with teary eyes. {name} decides to forgive him, and that evening they wave goodbye to the balloon together, imagining where it might land.

{name}'s best friend tells the class {name}'s embarrassing nickname from preschool, and everyone laughs. {name} feels hurt and stays away for days. When the friend apologizes sincerely, {name} explains how much it hurt, and then chooses to forgive. Their friendship comes back, a little stronger and more careful.

{name} helps Grandma in the vegetable patch and finds wriggly earthworms in the soil. {name} wants to throw them away, but Grandma explains that worms make the soil soft and help the purple eggplants grow. {name} gently puts each worm back and gives them the name 'garden helpers'.

In summer, red land crabs cross a coastal road to release their eggs in the sea. {name} joins volunteers in reflective vests who help the crabs cross safely and remind drivers to slow down. By dawn, {name} has counted over a hundred crabs reaching the waves.

Pangolin rolls into a ball every time the forest gets noisy with trash and loud music. The squirrels think he's just shy. {name} helps the animals pick up the litter and turn the music down, and Pangolin finally uncurls to show everyone the ant hill he has been guarding.

For the first time, {name} goes alone into the little shop next door to buy eggs while Mom waits right outside the glass door. {name}'s voice wobbles when asking the shopkeeper, and the coins slip once. But {name} counts them again, says thank you, and carries the eggs out proudly.

Little Sparrow is too scared to sing because the big birds are so loud. When a storm comes and a baby duckling gets lost in the reeds, only Sparrow's high, clear voice can be heard over the wind. {name} helps Sparrow keep calling until the mother duck follows the song and finds her baby.

{name} has to speak in front of the class about a favorite thing: Grandma's old wooden spinning top. {name}'s knees shake and the words disappear. {name} takes a breath, spins the top instead, and as it hums on the desk, the words come back one by one.

Every afternoon an old man plays Chinese chess alone in the park, and kids say he's strange. {name} notices he always sets up a second cup of tea. {name} sits down and asks to learn, and the man shares that his old chess friend moved away. Soon the bench has two players again.

Big Elephant wants to help everyone, but he keeps squashing the mouse's garden by accident and gets upset when Mouse is angry. {name} helps Elephant see the garden from Mouse's tiny height. Elephant learns to walk carefully on the path, and he waters the garden with his trunk.

Baby cousin cries and cries at the family dinner. {name} covers {his} ears at first, then wonders what the baby is feeling. Is baby hungry? Tired? Too noisy? {name} turns down the toy music and sings a soft song, and the baby yawns.

{name} spends all morning building a sandcastle at the beach, and a friend running by accidentally stomps on the tower. {name} shouts and turns away. Later the friend comes back with a bucket and says sorry. {name} feels the anger melt, and they build an even bigger castle together.

Two river otters argue over a shiny stone, and Big Otter pushes Little Otter into the cold water. Big Otter feels sorry but is too proud to say so. {name} helps him find words, and when he says 'I'm sorry, I was wrong,' Little Otter shares the stone and they slide down the bank together.

{name}'s younger sibling scribbles on {name}'s finished school poster the night before it's due. {name} is furious and says hurtful things. Later {name} notices the scribbles were hearts and the word 'best', and they redo the poster together, adding a small heart in the corner.

Every day the mail carrier rides a green scooter up {name}'s street, even in the rain. {name} decides to say thank you in a special way: a drawing of the green scooter with a rainbow, taped to the mailbox. The next day, there's a little note back that says 'Thank you too!'

Young Sparrow eats rice from the terraced fields all year but never thinks about where it comes from. When a drought comes, Sparrow sees the old water buffalo and the farmer working day and night. {name} and Sparrow help carry water, and at harvest Sparrow sings for the whole field.

Before bed, {name} remembers the warm dumplings Grandma made, the story Dad read, and the hug from a friend at school. With Mom, {name} whispers a soft thank-you for each, and with every thank-you a star seems to light up outside the window until {name} is fast asleep.

{name} promises the neighbor to water her tomato plants during her trip. On the third day, friends invite {name} to the water park. {name} remembers the wilting tomatoes, waters them first, and runs to catch up, arriving a little late but with a clear heart. The neighbor returns with the first red tomato.

Old Tortoise promises to deliver Owl's message to the far side of the forest before the full moon. On the way, the monkeys invite him to a fruit party. {name} walks beside Tortoise, who says 'a promise is a promise,' and they reach the meadow just as the moon rises.

{name} promises the retiring school janitor to keep the little garden behind the gym alive. When the rainy season floods it, {name} gathers friends, digs a drainage path, and replants the flowers. On the janitor's visit, the garden is blooming, with a new sign: 'Uncle Chen's Garden'.

{name} wants to tie {his} own shoelaces before the class field trip, but the loops keep falling apart. Grandma teaches a bunny-ears rhyme, and {name} practices on a cardboard shoe every evening. On the morning of the trip, {name} ties both shoes alone and races out the door.

In a mountain cave, a tiny water drop wants to make a hole in a big stone. The stone laughs. Drop after drop, season after season, the drop keeps falling. Years later, {name} visits the cave and finds a smooth little pool in the stone, where the water drop sparkles.

{name} wants to fold a paper crane for Grandma in the hospital, but the folds keep tearing and the wings come out crooked. After watching a video and practicing with scrap paper all week, {name} finally folds a perfect crane, and then a second one for the nurse.

{name} writes with the left hand, and a classmate says it's wrong. {name} feels embarrassed until the teacher shows famous left-handed artists and athletes. {name} helps the class set up a special left-handed scissors corner, and now everyone knows it's just another way to do things.

In the forest choir, Owl hoots, Crow caws and Bulbul whistles, and each says their song is the best. The music is a mess. {name} suggests they take turns and then sing together, and the forest fills with the most beautiful song any of them has heard.

{name}'s new classmate wears hearing aids, and some kids talk behind her back. {name} remembers how Grandma uses one too and how she reads lips. {name} learns a few sign language words from Grandma and teaches them to the class, and soon the new classmate is teaching everyone more.

{name} becomes the class turtle helper for a week. Feeding is fun, but cleaning the tank is not. When {name} forgets one day, the water gets cloudy and the turtle hides. {name} makes a picture chart to remember, and the turtle comes out to sunbathe again.

{name} loses a library book and wants to pretend it was never borrowed. Instead {name} tells the librarian, searches every corner of home, and offers to use pocket money to replace it. The book turns up under the car seat, and the librarian thanks {name} for being honest and responsible.

Little Bee is given the job of guarding the hive door, but gets distracted by a beautiful butterfly. A wasp almost sneaks in. {name} helps Little Bee sound the alarm in time, and Little Bee learns that every small job matters to the whole hive.

{name}'s class practices a dragon dance for the school festival, but everyone runs at their own speed and the dragon keeps twisting into a knot. {name} suggests they follow one drum beat. Step by step, the dragon starts to swirl, and on festival day it dances like it's alive.

Fox, Rabbit, Hedgehog and {name} each think they can cross the stream alone, and each falls in. Then they notice what each is good at: Fox finds the log, Rabbit hops to check the stones, Hedgehog's spines hold the rope. Together they build a bridge that everyone can cross.

Mom is sick, so {name}, Dad and big sister cook dinner together. Dad chops, sister stirs, and {name} washes the vegetables and sets the table. The noodles are a little too salty, but Mom smiles and says it's the best dinner because everyone made it together.

{name}'s toy dinosaur has a big toothy grin, and {name} brushes the dinosaur's teeth every night before {his} own. Tonight the dinosaur seems to say, 'Your turn!' {name} brushes up, down and around, and grins back at the mirror with sparkly teeth.

The moon peeks in the bathroom window while {name} takes a warm bath. Splash, splash, then a fluffy towel, cozy pajamas, and a sip of water. One by one, {name} says goodnight to the moon, the stars and the rubber duck, and snuggles into bed.

Dad makes steamed fish for dinner, and {name} is worried about the tiny bones. Dad shows how to eat slowly, pick out bones with chopsticks, and take small bites. {name} finds the first bone all alone and proudly puts it on the bone plate, then asks for another piece.

In art class, {name} makes a clay turtle, and {his} hands are covered in sticky gray clay. Before snack time, {name} follows the five-step handwashing poster: wet, soap, scrub, rinse, dry. The clay swirls down the drain, and {name} eats {his} snack with squeaky clean hands.

{name} has a small cavity and needs a filling. In the waiting room {name}'s heart is pounding. The dentist explains each tool, lets {name} raise a hand to pause, and plays {name}'s favorite song. It's over sooner than expected, and {name} chooses a dinosaur sticker.

At the beach, {name} sees a red flag flying and asks why the lifeguard won't let people swim there. The lifeguard explains rip currents that can pull swimmers out to sea. {name} and Dad move to the swimming area between the flags, and {name} teaches a cousin the flag rules.

Every morning, Grandpa Wang, the school crossing guard, holds up his big stop sign. {name} learns to wait for his whistle, look both ways, and walk with friends in the crosswalk. On the last day of school, the class gives Grandpa Wang a thank-you card shaped like a stop sign.

At kindergarten, the teacher teaches an earthquake song: 'Drop down low, cover your head, hold on tight like a little turtle!' During the drill, {name} and friends practice under the tables, and {name} helps a younger child remember the turtle pose.

Before going into the big supermarket, Mom and {name} pick a meeting spot: the red balloon sign by the checkout. When {name} gets distracted by the toy aisle and can't see Mom, {name} remembers, goes to the red balloon, and tells the cashier, who helps call Mom over.

{name} sees a phone charger dangling from the wall and wants to play with the cord. Dad explains that plugs and cords carry electricity and only grown-ups unplug them. {name} becomes the family's 'cord checker', telling Dad whenever a cord is hanging where little hands could reach.

When the block tower falls for the third time, {name}'s face gets red and hot. {name} wants to throw the blocks. Mom shows a squishy 'angry pillow' to squeeze, and they breathe like a big balloon together. When {name} feels calm, they build the tower again, wider at the bottom.

There's only one red tricycle at the playground, and {name} and a friend both want it. They pull and pull, and nobody rides. {name} has an idea: one rides, one pushes the bell, then switch. Ding, ding! The tricycle goes around and around with two happy friends.

At night, the closet door looks like a monster's mouth. {name} calls Dad, and together they open it with a flashlight: just jackets, shoes, and a teddy bear that fell down. {name} puts the teddy bear on guard duty, and the closet looks friendly now.

{name} practices hard for the class spelling contest but misses a word in the first round. {name} wants to hide under the desk. Then {name} cheers on the classmates still spelling, and after school writes the missed word ten times, ready for next time.

On a quiet night at Grandpa's countryside house, {name} lies on a mat looking up at the stars. A shooting star zips across the sky, and {name} makes a wish to come back next summer. As crickets sing softly, {name}'s eyes close under the twinkling sky.

A polar bear cub thinks she is too small to help her family catch fish through the ice. {name} notices she can hear the tiny cracks in the ice that the big bears miss. Her sharp ears warn the family of thin ice, and she learns that being small can be a strength.

A proud seagull laughs at the slow little hermit crab for carrying its home on its back. When a big wave crashes over the rocks, the seagull's nest is washed away, but the hermit crab simply tucks into its shell. {name} helps both of them, and the seagull learns not to judge others by how fast they are.

Vegetables keep disappearing from {name}'s apartment rooftop garden. {name} and a neighbor set up a detective watch and discover a family of birds and one clever squirrel. Instead of chasing them away, they build a small feeder so everyone shares the garden.

At the zoo, {name} wishes to be as tall as the giraffe. The giraffe can reach the treetop leaves, but can't see the little ladybug on the ground that {name} found. {name} decides being small is fun too, and waves to the giraffe from down below.

Since the baby came, Mom reads to the baby at bedtime and {name} feels left out. So Mom and {name} make a new plan: {name} reads the baby a picture book first, then Mom reads {name} a special big-kid story. {name} falls asleep feeling like the best big sibling.
